To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) a high dose of chemotherapy with stem cell transplantation is not more effective than conventional chemotherapy in patients with breast cancer; 2) there is a high risk of severe complications, such as heart failure, after a high dose of treatment; 3) there is no difference in the risk of severe complications in women treated with a high dose and those treated with conventional chemotherapy.
the use of a dose-intensive regimen with autologous stem cell support in the adjuvant setting for women with early breast cancer is not recommended.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the use of the autologous bone marrow transplantation in the treatment of patients with advanced breast cancer.
the study of the mechanisms of the antitumor effect of high-dose chemotherapy (HDC).
the development of a new treatment for advanced breast cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the evidence does not support a role for dose-intensive chemotherapy in the treatment of metastatic breast cancer.

the evidence for the use of dose intensified chemotherapy with autologous bone marrow support in breast cancer is weak and inconclusive, and therefore the use of this approach in the management of breast cancer cannot currently be justified.
the results of dose intensive therapy with autotransplantation for breast cancer are promising, but that more randomized studies are needed to determine the exact place of this approach.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the use of dose intensive therapy followed by autologous blood-stem-cell transplantation (ASCT) in patients with breast cancer who are in first or second remission does not increase the rate of relapse-free or overall survival compared to conventional-dose chemotherapy.
the results of dose intense therapy with autologus blood stem cell transplantation (ASCT) in breast cancer are encouraging.
the use of high dose therapy with autologouos stem cell transplantation (ASCT) in patients with breast cancer has not been shown to improve overall survival.
The main takeaway from our work is that

there is no evidence to support the routine use of autologous bone marrow transplantation in breast cancer patients, either for patients with metastatic disease or for those at high risk of relapse following primary treatment.
the current standard of care for breast cancer is not optimal, and that we can do a lot better for patients with this devastating disease.
the current standard of care is not sufficient.
